summary: Cameroon routes almost every nationality through its official eVisa portal (evisacam.cm) — you apply online and the approved visa is issued on arrival or at an embassy — while citizens of fellow CEMAC states (Chad, CAR, Congo, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea) and Nigeria enter visa-free.

notes: The UK government's travel advice says it is illegal to buy, sell, kill or capture any protected wild animal or trade its parts without a licence, and that offenders can be prosecuted and imprisoned or fined.

payments.text: Canada's travel advice says Cameroon is largely a cash-based economy and that credit cards are rarely accepted outside international hotels. The UK government says shops usually want small notes, which can be hard to get, that ATMs are not often available outside large towns, and that euros and US dollars are the most widely accepted foreign currencies.

safety.text: Most visits to Douala, Yaoundé and the coast are trouble-free, but governments advise against travel to the Far North (Boko Haram activity), the Northwest and Southwest regions (armed separatist conflict) and border areas with Chad and the Central African Republic. Petty crime and road accidents are the main everyday risks.

tips.text: The UK, Canadian and Australian governments advise against all travel to the North-West and South-West regions and the Far North. The UK makes exceptions around Maroua and advises against all but essential travel to Limbé, and also against all travel to the Bakassi Peninsula and within 40 km of the borders with Nigeria (except Garoua), Chad and the Central African Republic.

Cameroon has moved visa issuance online: apply only on the official evisacam.cm portal and ignore third-party visa websites. The approved eVisa is issued on arrival at Douala, Yaoundé-Nsimalen or Garoua airports, or at an embassy.
Keep your yellow fever certificate with your passport: it is required of every traveller aged 1 year or over.

The UK government's travel advice says to avoid travelling at night, particularly in rural areas, as many roads are unlit and in poor condition, and that police and gendarmerie roadblocks are common. Always carry ID — a residence permit or a certified copy of your passport showing a valid visa; the UK says police can detain you without it.

The UK government's travel advice says shops usually want small notes, which can be hard to obtain, that ATMs are not often available outside large towns, and that euros and US dollars are the most widely accepted foreign currencies.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Cameroon?
faq.answer: Almost certainly yes. Only citizens of the CEMAC bloc (Chad, Central African Republic, Congo, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea) and Nigeria enter visa-free; everyone else applies in advance on the official eVisa portal, evisacam.cm, and receives the visa on arrival or at an embassy.

faq.question: Does Cameroon offer a visa on arrival?
faq.answer: Not without prior approval. You must apply and be approved on evisacam.cm before traveling; the physical visa is then issued when you land at Douala, Yaoundé-Nsimalen or Garoua. Turning up with no eVisa approval risks being refused boarding or entry.

faq.question: How much does the Cameroon eVisa cost?
faq.answer: The online processing fee is 153 EUR for a short-stay visa (1 to 180 days), 229 EUR for an express short-stay visa, 305 EUR for a long-stay visa (181 to 360 days) and 153 EUR for a transit visa. It is paid on evisacam.cm and is not refunded if the visa is refused.

faq.question: Is the yellow fever vaccine mandatory for Cameroon?
faq.answer: Yes — proof of yellow fever vaccination is required for all travellers aged 1 year or over, regardless of where they are arriving from.

faq.question: Is Cameroon safe for tourists?
faq.answer: Parts of it are not. The UK, Canadian and Australian governments advise against all travel to the North-West, South-West and Far North regions; the UK advises against all but essential travel to Limbé and the North Region, including Garoua. Canada says violent crime occurs frequently, especially at night, in major cities and on main roads. Check your government's latest travel advice before booking.
